scope: Read-only editorial and graph-necessity audit; canonical Composer General Economics membership only

wording_findings.title: Wrong article before country names
wording_findings.quote: A Arden report / A Estara report / A Ilyria report
wording_findings.why: The article is grammatically wrong; the country-name substitution is conspicuous. The plural product modifiers also sound stiff.
wording_findings.suggestion: Use “A report in Arden opposes opening the market for solar panels to international trade because domestic producers would lose.” Use the corresponding country, good, and losing group in each item. Retain the equations and compensation assumptions.

wording_findings.title: Wrong article before eight dollars
wording_findings.quote: a $8 tariff / a $8 per-unit tariff
wording_findings.why: Eight starts with a vowel sound.
wording_findings.suggestion: Use “an $8 tariff” or “an $8 per-unit tariff.”

wording_findings.title: Repetitive correction prompt and imprecise curve language
wording_findings.quote: Straight domestic supply and demand each change by one unit ... What is the correct correction?
wording_findings.why: The closing phrase is tautological. Quantities supplied and demanded change as price changes; the sentence loosely says supply and demand themselves change. Keyed choices also end in “leaving $64 destroyed,” which sounds unnatural.
wording_findings.suggestion: For L-062: “For each $1 increase in price, quantity supplied rises by one unit and quantity demanded falls by one unit. A report describes the entire $368 loss of consumer surplus as deadweight loss. Which statement correctly separates transfers from deadweight loss?” In the key use “... and $112 is a gain in producer surplus, leaving $64 in deadweight loss.” Preserve each item’s numbers.

wording_findings.title: Ledger and imports used as shorthand
wording_findings.quote: A tariff is chosen to leave 24 imports. Which ledger follows ...?
wording_findings.why: “Leave 24 imports” omits units; “which ledger follows” sounds like an internal accounting instruction instead of a question.
wording_findings.suggestion: “The government sets a tariff that reduces imports to 24 units. With the world price unchanged, which option correctly gives the tariff per unit, government revenue, and deadweight loss?” Adapt the import target for each item.

wording_findings.title: Welfare ledger wording
wording_findings.quote: Which complete import, revenue and distortion ledger is correct? / Which welfare ledger is correct?
wording_findings.why: The calculation is appropriate; “complete ... ledger” adds unnecessary accounting language.
wording_findings.suggestion: “Which option correctly reports imports, tariff revenue, and the production and consumption losses?” Where total deadweight loss is listed, mention that total as well. Use “market for coffee beans,” “market for medical gloves,” etc., instead of plural nouns stacked before “market.”

wording_findings.title: Reversed attribution wording
wording_findings.quote: before crediting protection to infant-industry learning
wording_findings.why: The intended question is whether protection caused additional learning and justified its costs. The phrase reverses the attribution.
wording_findings.suggestion: “What additional evidence is needed to show that protection encouraged learning and that the resulting benefits justified its costs?” Keep the comparison with unprotected firms and new machinery.

wording_findings.title: Incomplete description of linear curves
wording_findings.quote: unchanged and straight / straight domestic curves / straight curves
wording_findings.why: “Linear demand and supply curves” is the familiar economic description. The word “curves” should not be omitted when describing their shape.
wording_findings.suggestion: Use “The domestic demand and supply curves are linear and remain unchanged.” Keep the unchanged world-price assumption wherever present.

wording_findings.title: Reciprocal terminology foregrounded instead of the economic task
wording_findings.quote: reciprocal costs of 1 Y / reciprocal opportunity cost / reciprocal-rate assessment
wording_findings.why: Reciprocals are the arithmetic method. The natural task is to calculate opportunity cost or evaluate the terms of trade in the requested units.
wording_findings.suggestion: H-007: “What is each producer’s opportunity cost of one unit of Y, measured in units of X?” M-009: “What is the opportunity cost of one bowl, measured in mugs?” EL-001: “Express the offered exchange rate in signs per badge. Which producer should export badges, and would both gain?”

wording_findings.title: Compressed strict-gains phrasing
wording_findings.quote: strict mutual-gain rates / strict price range / which strict range is equivalent?
wording_findings.why: The strict inequalities matter, but the noun phrases are awkward. L-014 also uses count-like “1 cocoa” and “3 tea,” and does not identify what the range is equivalent to.
wording_findings.suggestion: Ask for “the range of trading prices that makes both producers better off than producing the good themselves,” excluding break-even endpoints. For L-014 specify units of cocoa and tea and ask directly for the mutually beneficial range in units of cocoa per unit of tea. Preserve the shipping cost in L-007 and the reciprocal units.

wording_findings.title: Ledger metaphor in prose
wording_findings.quote: Within the gross ledger / not included in the first ledger
wording_findings.why: The metaphor makes the welfare accounting harder to follow than naming the estimate.
wording_findings.suggestion: LB-003: “Before adjustment costs, consumers gain $160 million and displaced workers lose $60 million.” B3-052: “These export losses are additional to the gains and losses already listed.” In LB-003’s key replace “feasible in this ledger” with “feasible under the stated estimates.” Preserve the distinction between domestic transfers and real costs.

wording_findings.title: Missing antecedent and awkward fairness phrase
wording_findings.quote: They agree on effects but rank fairness differently. What differs?
wording_findings.why: A standalone question never identifies “they.” “Rank fairness” does not clearly describe the value disagreement.
wording_findings.suggestion: “Two economists agree on a policy’s effects but place different weight on fairness when judging the policy. What explains their different recommendations?”

wording_findings.title: Telegraphic policy-analysis prompts
wording_findings.quote: rank equity differently / Must economist disagreement be political? / What should advice report?
wording_findings.why: These are understandable but read like compressed notes.
wording_findings.suggestion: M-007: “Two advisers agree on the predicted effects but place different weight on equity. What explains their disagreement?” R-039: “Must disagreement between economists reflect different political views?” BR-041: “A model’s conclusion depends on a particular assumption. What should an economist explain when using the model to advise policymakers?”

wording_findings.title: Vague uncertainty terminology
wording_findings.quote: confidence range
wording_findings.why: This is less precise than “confidence interval,” but the item tests uncertainty rather than statistical interval construction.
wording_findings.suggestion: “A forecast gives a range of possible effects rather than a single estimate. What does the range acknowledge?” Use “confidence interval” only if that statistical concept is intended and taught.

wording_findings.title: Assessment-writing language inside the question
wording_findings.quote: Which paired equilibrium prediction completes the reasoning?
wording_findings.why: The phrase describes the assessment design rather than asking the economics question directly.
wording_findings.suggestion: “Demand shifts to the right while supply remains unchanged. What happens to equilibrium price and quantity?”

wording_findings.title: Compressed incentive language in stem and answer
wording_findings.quote: limiting selection / poor-fit jobs / substitution into a different undesirable action
wording_findings.why: The concrete problem is providers choosing easy clients or drivers accepting unsuitable deliveries and canceling. The abstract phrasing obscures it.
wording_findings.suggestion: EL-003: “Which redesign would reward successful placements without encouraging providers to avoid clients who need more support?” M-008: use “delivery requests they are unlikely to complete.” Key: “The reward encourages drivers to accept requests to improve their rating, then cancel them later.”

wording_findings.title: Undefined decision margin
wording_findings.quote: Which margin does the rule most directly target? / Which margin is most directly affected?
wording_findings.why: “Margin” is legitimate economics language, but here “decision” is clearer and loses none of the intended incentive analysis.
wording_findings.suggestion: “Which decision does the rule most directly influence?” Retain the cancellation deadline and the twelve-month loyalty threshold.

wording_findings.title: Unnatural airline phrasing
wording_findings.quote: displaces cargo margin of $170 / next flight frequency
wording_findings.why: Both compress the actual action into business shorthand.
wording_findings.suggestion: H-007: “Carrying the passenger means giving up $170 in net earnings from cargo.” L-007: “Adding one more flight would generate $80,000 in revenue...” Retain the operating costs and delay costs imposed on other flights.

wording_findings.title: Unexplained common scoring units
wording_findings.quote: supplies costing 42 points / leaving staff in readiness
wording_findings.why: Supplies normally have money costs. A points-based comparison can work, but the common valuation scale and standby alternative should be explicit.
wording_findings.suggestion: Introduce: “A hospital evaluates all benefits and costs using the same points scale.” Refer to “a 42-point supply cost” and “keeping staff available for emergencies, valued at 35 points.” Preserve 88, 42, 35, the 8-point saving, and the 12-point benefit reduction; do not silently convert the units to dollars.

wording_findings.title: Unnatural marginal-analysis closing
wording_findings.quote: The marginal social decision is:
wording_findings.why: Marginal social benefit and cost are standard terms; “the marginal social decision” is not a natural question.
wording_findings.suggestion: “Taking all the listed benefits and costs into account, should the hospital add the test?” Preserve the inclusion of expected false-positive follow-up costs.

wording_findings.title: Strict comparison expressed awkwardly
wording_findings.quote: begin to set the opportunity cost strictly instead of B
wording_findings.why: The question concerns which alternative has greater net value. Expressing that directly preserves the strict inequality.
wording_findings.suggestion: “For what values of x would C have a higher net value than B and therefore determine A’s opportunity cost?” Keep the tie at x = 15 distinct from x > 15.

wording_findings.title: Vague evaluative closings
wording_findings.quote: Which claim is safest? / Which assessment is exact?
wording_findings.why: These ask students to infer what “safest” or “exact” means.
wording_findings.suggestion: Use “Which conclusion is supported?” and “Which statement correctly distinguishes the predictions from the board’s value judgment?” In TRADE-L-021’s key, “Both can gain through specialization without either producer specializing completely” is more natural than “without universal complete specialization.”

wording_findings.title: Dense tax-burden language
wording_findings.quote: seller-burden rectangle / combined buyer- and seller-burden rectangle / tax burden per continuing unit
wording_findings.why: The distinction between tax payments and lost gains from trade is important, but the wording stacks several abstractions. ELITE-318 has no image, making “rectangle” especially unnecessary.
wording_findings.suggestion: ELITE-318 and HARD-276: “On the units still sold after the tax, what is the sellers’ total loss from receiving a lower price? Exclude surplus lost on sales that no longer occur.” HARD-277: ask for “total tax revenue,” retaining the link to the combined burden if that is the objective. HARD-279: use “tax burden per unit still sold” and “total sales revenue after paying the tax.” Keep all welfare exclusions; do not replace the question with total producer-surplus loss.

graph_findings.reason: The first two stems already identify the bowed shape; the third states that opportunity cost rises and asks why. Increasing opportunity cost and resource suitability answer these questions without reading a plotted point.
graph_findings.action: Either keep as conceptual questions with optional illustrations, or remove the stated shape/direction and ask students to compare opportunity costs between labeled segments.

graph_findings.reason: 9017 explicitly contrasts a move between demand curves with a move along one curve. 40008 already names a decrease in supply. Their keyed conceptual distinctions require no coordinates or visible geometry.
graph_findings.action: Ask which labeled movement is a shift, without naming it in the stem; alternatively retain the concept question and treat the graph as illustrative.

graph_findings.reason: The choices themselves say “along PPF0,” “on PPF0,” or “beyond PPF0.” Only the beyond-frontier choice requires greater capacity. No plotted location must be read.
graph_findings.action: Offer labeled points only, so the student must identify the point outside the frontier.

graph_findings.reason: The stems explicitly disclose that the country imports or exports. In the intended competitive trade model, that already determines whether the world price is below or above the no-trade price.
graph_findings.action: Ask students to read the no-trade price and compare it with the world price, without disclosing the resulting trade direction.

graph_findings.reason: The stem gives the $3 equilibrium and asks about $2 and $4. Standard shortage/surplus price adjustment identifies the key without the image.
graph_findings.action: Ask for the size of each imbalance, with plausible numerical distractors, or keep the qualitative question with an optional graph.

graph_findings.reason: The stem gives both after-tax prices and quantity; statutory tax equivalence answers the question without the image. Indeed the qualitative no-change answer requires none of those numbers.
graph_findings.action: Retain as a conceptual tax-equivalence question without a required graph, or require students to read the prices and quantity and select among internally consistent numerical outcomes.

graph_findings.reason: “Beyond the lower posted price” already describes an effective ceiling. The key asks only about nonprice rationing following excess demand; no plotted number is used.
graph_findings.action: If graph reasoning is intended, ask for the shortage or another graph-derived quantity before the rationing inference.

graph_findings.reason: Only the key correctly combines a ceiling below equilibrium with binding status, or a floor above equilibrium with binding status. The other choices contradict the definition or misidentify a legal maximum/minimum. In 40021/40027 the stem additionally announces “binding.” The graph-specific distance or price relation can be accepted from the key without being verified.
graph_findings.action: Provide at least two logically valid policy/price explanations, such as “binding because below equilibrium” and “nonbinding because above equilibrium” for a ceiling. Use the graph to distinguish them; do not announce binding status when that is being tested.

graph_findings.reason: The determinant in each stem establishes the direction of demand change with supply fixed. Only the key describes that change; the other choices invoke the opposite demand change or a supply shift. The keyed P/Q labels need not be read.
graph_findings.action: Keep the stated determinant, but make at least two choices agree on the correct demand direction and differ in plotted starting or ending coordinates.

graph_findings.reason: 258 and 259 have only one choice with the correct general comparative-static prediction; the specific unchanged coordinate is bundled into it. In 265 only the key has the required price rise when demand rises and supply falls.
graph_findings.action: Give plausible alternatives with the same theoretically certain direction but different graph-specific outcomes for the ambiguous variable.

graph_findings.reason: Only the key combines unchanged demand with quantity demanded rising when price falls. In L-001 the survey rules out a shift and one of the remaining alternatives violates the law of demand. Students need not calculate the 125-thousand change or 25-thousand rate.
graph_findings.action: Make competing choices agree on movement along demand and increasing quantity demanded, but offer different graph-derived magnitudes.

graph_findings.reason: Only one option describes a theoretically valid movement along the named curve; alternatives incorrectly call it a curve shift or reverse the law of demand/supply.
graph_findings.action: Include both valid directions of movement along the same curve, so A and B must be located on the graph.

graph_findings.reason: Only one option is a demand shifter: consumer income. The other choices concern own-price movements or producers. The student can choose income without seeing whether the demand curve moved left or right.
graph_findings.action: Offer both higher and lower consumer income, plus other plausible demand shifters, so the displayed direction matters.

graph_findings.reason: Wrong choices confuse shifts and movements or give a quantity response opposite to the law of demand/supply. Only the key survives that conceptual check; its final quantity or slope can be selected without measurement.
graph_findings.action: Use alternatives that preserve the correct shift/movement distinction and price-response direction but differ in quantities, slopes, or how much the later movement offsets the shift.

graph_findings.reason: B3-054 has only one choice treating domestic auction proceeds as a domestic gain without removing unchanged distortions. H-015 is answered by the general rule that government auctions of import rights generate revenue; rectangle R adds no tested numerical information. In L-099 the distractors deny the foreign rent transfer, call it destroyed world surplus, or explicitly double-count it.
graph_findings.action: For B3-054 and L-099 keep the same correct welfare logic in at least two options and vary graph-derived rent/loss amounts. H-015 can be a conceptual question, or can ask for both auction revenue and the remaining deadweight loss.

graph_findings.reason: 40007 offers only one valid determinant/shift relationship. 40010 offers only one valid demand-increase explanation consistent with unchanged production conditions. 40011 already asks about a demand shift along supply and only the key describes that. In 40014/40016 the stated determinants eliminate the other explanations before the endpoint values are checked.
graph_findings.action: Use economically coherent distractors and make their distinguishing features depend on labeled endpoints or the plotted sizes of changes.

graph_findings.reason: 9003 practically discloses that the first move raises output without a tradeoff; the alternatives confuse resource use, growth, and attainability. In MEDIUM-150, the distractors explicitly label an inside point efficient, treat greater output as proof of efficiency, or wrongly exclude frontier endpoints. In 40004, the alternatives incorrectly equate a frontier movement with capacity growth or a shift with unemployment.
graph_findings.action: Use choices with plausible point classifications or comparable explanations that differ in what the graph actually shows. For MEDIUM-150, lists of point labels would require inspection without the false explanatory cues.

graph_findings.reason: The options disclose the $30 equilibrium. Comparing the $50 ceiling or $10 floor with that supplied value identifies the key.
graph_findings.action: Remove the equilibrium value from the choices or give competing internally consistent numerical outcomes that must be checked against the graph.

graph_findings.reason: 40038 has only one internally correct elasticity/burden relationship. 40044 has only one defensible explanation of shared tax incidence; other options claim no wedge or automatic all-or-nothing burdens. 40047 has only one option consistent with both buyer remittance and the less-elastic side bearing more. The plotted burden split is not needed to select these keys.
graph_findings.action: Use at least two economically consistent burden/elasticity statements, one matching the graph and one not. Keep legal remittance the same across options where it is supplied in the stem.

graph_findings.reason: HARD-278’s other options use original quantity, the entire tax instead of the buyer share, or sellers’ receipts. HARD-281’s other explanations conflate legal incidence or full prices with burden. STX-EL-001 supplies $7.50 + $6 in the stem and the $10.50 reference price in every option; $13.50 including tax and a $3/$3 split follow without the graph.
graph_findings.action: Give multiple internally consistent calculations using plausible graph readings. For STX-EL-001, keep the pre-tax benchmark out of the options if students are meant to read it from the image.

evidence.stem: Refer to the graph. As production moves farther right along bowed PPF0, what happens to the opportunity cost of additional pizzas?
options: It falls as fewer robots are sacrificed per pizza
It rises as more robots are sacrificed per pizza
It stays constant at one robot for each pizza
It becomes zero after production reaches B
evidence.correct_option: It rises as more robots are sacrificed per pizza
evidence.feedback: The frontier becomes steeper as pizza production rises, showing increasing robot cost per pizza.

evidence.stem: Refer to the graph. Which proposed change would require greater productive capacity rather than reallocation along PPF0?
options: Moving from A to B along PPF0
Moving from B toward A along PPF0
Producing at a point beyond PPF0
Choosing another point located on PPF0
evidence.correct_option: Producing at a point beyond PPF0
evidence.feedback: Points on PPF0 are attainable now; sustaining a point outside requires an outward capacity shift.

evidence.stem: Refer to the graph. Which statement correctly distinguishes moving from A to B from shifting PPF0 to PPF1?
options: A to B reallocates; PPF1 expands capacity
Both changes expand productive capacity
A to B expands capacity; PPF1 shows unemployment
Both changes only reallocate current production
evidence.correct_option: A to B reallocates; PPF1 expands capacity
evidence.feedback: A and B share one frontier; the outward PPF1 expands feasible production.

evidence.stem: Refer to the graph. Equilibrium moves from A to B after one market determinant changes. Evaluate the graph evidence: which explanation identifies the curve shift and connects it to the new price and quantity?
options: Higher theater operating costs shift supply left, raising price and reducing quantity
A higher substitute price shifts demand left, raising price and reducing quantity
Higher consumer income shifts supply left for a normal good, reducing quantity
A lower ticket price shifts supply left as firms move along the demand curve
evidence.correct_option: Higher theater operating costs shift supply left, raising price and reducing quantity
evidence.feedback: Higher operating costs reduce supply, shifting it left from S0 to S1. With demand unchanged, the equilibrium moves from A to B: price rises and quantity falls.

evidence.stem: Refer to the graph. Why is the move from A to B a decrease in supply rather than merely a decrease in quantity supplied?
options: Supply itself shifts left from S0 to S1
Quantity supplied rises along the original S0 curve
Demand itself shifts right from D0 to D1
The market stays at A on the original curves
evidence.correct_option: Supply itself shifts left from S0 to S1
evidence.feedback: A quantity-supplied change moves along one curve; here the supply curve itself shifts.

evidence.stem: Refer to the movie-ticket graph. Streaming subscriptions are substitutes for theater visits. With production conditions unchanged, which event could take equilibrium from A to B?
options: Streaming subscriptions become more expensive, increasing demand for movie tickets.
Streaming subscriptions become cheaper, increasing demand for movie tickets.
The movie-ticket price rises by itself, shifting demand for movie tickets right.
Theaters face lower operating costs, shifting supply of movie tickets right.
evidence.correct_option: Streaming subscriptions become more expensive, increasing demand for movie tickets.
evidence.feedback: A lies on D0 and S0; B lies on D1 and S0. Demand has increased while supply stays fixed. A higher substitute price can cause that shift; the higher ticket price is a result, not a demand shifter.

evidence.stem: Refer to the graph. Which description correctly separates the demand shift from the movement along supply?
options: Quantity demanded rises only because price falls along D0
Supply shifts right and demand stays fixed
Both curves shift right equally
Demand shifts D0 to D1, and equilibrium moves upward along S0
evidence.correct_option: Demand shifts D0 to D1, and equilibrium moves upward along S0
evidence.feedback: Demand changes curves; the higher equilibrium is also a movement along unchanged supply.

evidence.stem: Refer to the movie-ticket graph. An analyst explains the move from B back to A by cheaper streaming substitutes and lower theater operating costs. Which evaluation uses both the determinants and the endpoints?
options: Inconsistent: cheaper substitutes increase movie demand, so both curves shift right.
Consistent: both demand and supply fall, leaving quantity fixed at 200 thousand.
Consistent: demand falls and supply rises; price falls $4 while quantity stays 200 thousand.
Inconsistent: unchanged quantity rules out any change in demand or supply.
evidence.correct_option: Consistent: demand falls and supply rises; price falls $4 while quantity stays 200 thousand.
evidence.feedback: Cheaper streaming substitutes reduce movie demand from D1 to D0; lower operating costs increase supply from S1 to S0. B is $14 and A is $10, both at 200 thousand. Opposing quantity effects offset here, though they need not do so in every market.

evidence.stem: Refer to the gasoline graph. Suppose cheaper alternative transportation reduces gasoline demand while refinery costs fall. If the curves change from those through B to those through D, which outcome and explanation fit?
options: Price falls by $2 and quantity stays 200; the two shifts have offsetting quantity effects.
Price stays $6 and quantity falls to 150; both shifts reduce equilibrium quantity.
Price falls by $2 and quantity rises to 250; the graph shows only a supply increase.
Price rises by $2 and quantity stays 200; both shifts raise equilibrium price.
evidence.correct_option: Price falls by $2 and quantity stays 200; the two shifts have offsetting quantity effects.
evidence.feedback: B is at price $6 and quantity 200; D is at $4 and 200. Demand falls and supply increases. Both reduce price, while their opposing quantity effects offset in this graph.

evidence.stem: Refer to the graph. Why is the $1,000 rent ceiling binding?
options: The ceiling is 500 dollars above equilibrium
The ceiling is 500 dollars below equilibrium
The ceiling exactly equals the equilibrium price
Supply exceeds demand at the ceiling price
evidence.correct_option: The ceiling is 500 dollars below equilibrium
evidence.feedback: A legal maximum below equilibrium blocks the clearing price.

evidence.stem: Refer to the graph. Why is the $15 minimum wage binding?
options: The floor is 3 dollars below equilibrium
The floor exactly equals the equilibrium wage
Labor demand exceeds labor supply at the floor
The floor is 3 dollars above equilibrium
evidence.correct_option: The floor is 3 dollars above equilibrium
evidence.feedback: The $15 minimum wage is $3 above the $12 equilibrium wage, so it prevents the labor market from clearing at equilibrium.

evidence.stem: Which elasticity inference fits the graph?
options: Supply is less elastic; buyers bear more
Demand is more elastic; buyers bear more
Demand is less elastic; buyers bear more
Elasticity is irrelevant to the burden split
evidence.correct_option: Demand is less elastic; buyers bear more
evidence.feedback: Demand is less elastic than supply in the graph, and buyers bear the larger share of the tax burden. Those two observations are consistent with the rule that the less elastic side bears more of a tax.

evidence.stem: Refer to the graph. Why does a tax imposed on sellers not mean sellers bear the entire $8 burden?
options: Market prices adjust so buyers bear $2 of the tax and sellers bear $6.
Sellers bear no burden whenever the supply curve shifts
Buyers must bear all 8 dollars because demand slopes down
No tax wedge exists at the new equilibrium quantity
evidence.correct_option: Market prices adjust so buyers bear $2 of the tax and sellers bear $6.
evidence.feedback: Statutory placement does not prevent prices from splitting the burden.

evidence.stem: Refer to the graph. The tax is legally imposed on buyers. Which statement correctly describes who remits the tax, who bears the economic burden, and what the burden split implies about elasticity?
options: Buyers remit the tax, bear all $8, and are more elastic.
Sellers remit the tax, bear $6, and are less elastic.
Sellers bear $2, implying perfectly elastic supply.
Buyers remit the tax, bear $6, and are less elastic.
evidence.correct_option: Buyers remit the tax, bear $6, and are less elastic.
evidence.feedback: The buyer-side tax is legally assigned to buyers, but prices split burden 6 to buyers and 2 to sellers.

evidence.stem: A market moves from $40 and 500 units before a tax to a buyer price of $46, seller receipt of $34, and 420 units afterward. What is the seller-burden rectangle on units still traded, excluding the surplus lost on missing trades?
evidence.feedback: The seller loses $40 − $34 = $6 per continuing unit, so the rectangle is $6 × 420 = $2,520. Using 500 applies the burden to trades that no longer occur. The $12 wedge times 420 is total revenue, not the seller share alone.

evidence.stem: A learner correctly identifies a rightward demand shift with supply fixed. Which paired equilibrium prediction completes the reasoning?
options: Both price and quantity rise
Both price and quantity fall
Price rises while quantity falls
Price falls while quantity rises
evidence.correct_option: Both price and quantity rise
evidence.feedback: A rightward demand shift creates upward pressure on both equilibrium price and equilibrium quantity when supply is fixed.

evidence.stem: Refer to the tax-incidence graph. The tax shown raises the buyer price to $18, lowers the seller price to $12, and reduces quantity to 80. If the same per-unit tax were legally imposed on buyers instead of sellers, what would change?
options: Nothing about the final buyer price, seller price, or quantity
Buyers would pay $12, sellers would receive $18, and quantity would remain 80
Buyers would bear the entire tax, so sellers would still receive $15
The tax wedge would disappear because supply would no longer shift
evidence.correct_option: Nothing about the final buyer price, seller price, or quantity
evidence.feedback: An equal per-unit tax creates the same wedge and equilibrium whether the law assigns payment to buyers or sellers.

evidence.stem: Refer to the graph. Starting at D1/S1, demand and supply both increase to D2/S2. Which explanation compares the general prediction with the particular equilibrium drawn?
options: Quantity rises for certain; price is generally ambiguous but remains at P2 in this drawing
Price rises for certain; quantity is generally ambiguous but remains at Q1 in this drawing
Both price and quantity are generally fixed because the curves shift together
Quantity falls for certain; price is generally ambiguous but falls to P1 here
evidence.correct_option: Quantity rises for certain; price is generally ambiguous but remains at P2 in this drawing
evidence.feedback: Both increases raise equilibrium quantity. Their price effects oppose, so theory alone leaves price ambiguous; the displayed intersections show P2 in both the initial and final equilibria.

evidence.stem: Refer to the graph. Demand increases from D1 to D2 while supply decreases from S2 to S1. Infer what theory guarantees, then use the plotted equilibria to explain the quantity outcome.
options: Price rises for certain; quantity is generally ambiguous but stays at Q2 in this drawing
Quantity rises for certain; price is generally ambiguous but stays at P2 in this drawing
Price falls for certain; quantity stays at Q2 because both curves shift right
Quantity falls for certain; price stays at P1 because the shifts offset
evidence.correct_option: Price rises for certain; quantity is generally ambiguous but stays at Q2 in this drawing
evidence.feedback: The demand increase and supply decrease both raise price. Their quantity effects oppose; the graph shows those effects offset at Q2 for this particular pair of shifts.

evidence.stem: Refer to the graph. The price of a substitute rises, shifting demand from D1 to D2 while supply remains S1. Which chain of graph evidence explains the resulting equilibrium change?
options: Demand shifts right; equilibrium moves from P2, Q1 to P3, Q2, so both price and quantity rise
Demand shifts left; equilibrium moves from P3, Q2 to P2, Q1, so both price and quantity fall
Supply shifts right; equilibrium moves from P2, Q1 to P1, Q2, so price falls as quantity rises
Supply shifts left; equilibrium moves from P2, Q3 to P3, Q2, so price rises as quantity falls
evidence.correct_option: Demand shifts right; equilibrium moves from P2, Q1 to P3, Q2, so both price and quantity rise
evidence.feedback: The higher substitute price increases demand. With supply fixed at S1, the graph moves from the D1/S1 intersection at P2, Q1 to the D2/S1 intersection at P3, Q2.

evidence.stem: Refer to the graph. A close substitute becomes cheaper, reducing demand from D2 to D1 while supply remains S2. Which explanation correctly traces the change in equilibrium?
options: Demand shifts left; equilibrium moves from P2, Q3 to P1, Q2, reducing both price and quantity
Demand shifts right; equilibrium moves from P1, Q2 to P2, Q3, increasing both price and quantity
Supply shifts left; equilibrium moves from P2, Q3 to P3, Q2, increasing price and reducing quantity
Supply shifts right; equilibrium moves from P3, Q2 to P2, Q3, reducing price and increasing quantity
evidence.correct_option: Demand shifts left; equilibrium moves from P2, Q3 to P1, Q2, reducing both price and quantity
evidence.feedback: A cheaper substitute reduces demand for this good. With S2 unchanged, the equilibrium moves from D2/S2 at P2, Q3 to D1/S2 at P1, Q2.

evidence.stem: Refer to the supply and demand shift graph. If demand increases and supply decreases, what does this graph show is possible?
options: Price rises while quantity stays the same
Price falls while quantity rises
Price stays the same while quantity rises
Price falls while quantity stays the same

evidence.stem: Refer to the tax incidence graph. What is the seller-burden rectangle on the units still traded, excluding surplus lost on missing trades?
evidence.feedback: The per-unit seller burden is $3 relative to the original $15 price. Multiplying by 80 continuing units gives $240. The full welfare loss for that side also includes surplus lost on trades that no longer occur.

evidence.stem: Refer to the tax incidence graph. What is the combined buyer- and seller-burden rectangle on units still traded, which becomes government revenue?
evidence.feedback: The $6 wedge applies to 80 continuing trades, so the rectangle is $480. This is the combined per-unit incidence times taxed quantity. Lost gains from the missing trades are additional welfare loss and are not government revenue.

evidence.stem: Refer to the tax incidence graph. For the units still purchased after the tax, what is the total extra payment by buyers relative to paying the original price for those same units? This question excludes the welfare effect of purchases forgone.
options: $300: $3 extra on the original 100 units.
$480: the full $6 tax on the remaining 80 units.
$240: $3 extra on the remaining 80 units.
$540: the change in sellers’ total receipts.
evidence.correct_option: $240: $3 extra on the remaining 80 units.
evidence.feedback: The buyer price rises from $15 to $18 and 80 units are purchased after tax. For these continuing purchases, the extra payment is ($18 - $15) x 80 = $240. Using all 100 original units includes purchases no longer made; using $6 assigns the seller burden to buyers.

evidence.stem: Refer to the tax incidence graph. A seller group divides the fall in total net-of-tax sales receipts by the 80 units still sold and calls the result its tax burden per continuing unit. Why is that calculation misleading?
options: The $540 receipt decline includes fewer units sold; the price burden on each continuing unit is $3.
The $540 receipt decline is entirely a price effect; the burden on each continuing unit is $6.75.
The $240 receipt decline includes fewer units sold; the price burden on each continuing unit is $6.
The $300 receipt decline is entirely a quantity effect; the price burden on each continuing unit is $0.
evidence.correct_option: The $540 receipt decline includes fewer units sold; the price burden on each continuing unit is $3.
evidence.feedback: Receipts fall from $15 x 100 = $1,500 to $12 x 80 = $960, a $540 decline. This combines $300 from 20 fewer units valued at the old price and $240 from receiving $3 less on each of 80 continuing sales. The per-unit seller tax burden is $15 - $12 = $3; gross receipts are not a measure of producer surplus.

evidence.stem: Refer to the tax graph. Using the original equilibrium as the benchmark, how is the per-unit tax burden divided?

Buyers bear $6 and sellers $0, because the buyer price is highest
Buyers bear $0 and sellers $6, because the shifted curve is supply
Buyers bear $18 and sellers $12, equal to the two after-tax prices
evidence.correct_option: Buyers bear $3 and sellers $3, so each bears half
evidence.feedback: The original price is $15. Buyers now pay $18, an increase of $3, while sellers keep $12, a decrease of $3. These burdens sum to the $6 wedge. Neither legal remittance nor the full price level measures incidence.

evidence.stem: Refer to the PPF graph. Production first moves from F to C and then from C to D, with resources and technology unchanged. Why does only the second move clearly sacrifice Y for more X?

The first creates growth; growth eliminates opportunity cost on the second
F is unattainable, so its output cannot be compared with C
D lies inside the frontier and therefore wastes Y
evidence.correct_option: The first uses slack to raise both outputs; the second reallocates along the frontier
evidence.feedback: F to C raises both outputs by improving use of existing capacity. C to D moves between efficient frontier points, gaining X at the expense of Y.

evidence.stem: Refer to the PPF graph. Why does the opportunity cost of Good X rise as production moves from A toward E?

Resources are increasingly less suited to producing additional X
The economy has escaped scarcity by moving along the curve

evidence.stem: Refer to the supply and demand graph with D1, D2, S1, and S2. Which comparison best captures the difference between moving from D1 to D2 and moving along D1?

evidence.correct_option: More than one-sixth and less than one-third
evidence.feedback: Reverse both the goods and the ratio when changing opportunity-cost orientation.

evidence.stem: A technology has increasing rather than constant opportunity cost. Which claim is safest?
options: Comparative advantage can guide reallocation without universal complete specialization
Both producers must always specialize completely.
Opportunity cost becomes irrelevant after exchange
Absolute advantage fixes every output
evidence.correct_option: Comparative advantage can guide reallocation without universal complete specialization
evidence.feedback: With increasing opportunity cost, producing more of a good requires giving up progressively more of the other good. Reallocation can create gains while relative marginal costs differ, but the rising cost can make further specialization unattractive before either producer specializes completely. Absolute productivity alone does not determine that stopping point.

evidence.stem: If one mug costs a studio 2 bowls, what is the reciprocal opportunity cost of one bowl?
options: One-half mug
Two mugs.
Four mugs
One mug
evidence.correct_option: One-half mug
evidence.feedback: Reverse both the goods and the ratio when changing opportunity-cost orientation.

evidence.stem: A model works only under one assumption. What should advice report?
options: Report only the baseline result
Drop the assumption from the analysis
How the conclusion changes when the assumption changes
Delay all advice until the assumption can be proven true.
evidence.correct_option: How the conclusion changes when the assumption changes
evidence.feedback: Responsible advice reports assumptions, uncertainty, and plausible unintended consequences.

evidence.stem: A projection includes a confidence range. What does it acknowledge?
options: The true effect is guaranteed to lie inside the range
Uncertainty in the predicted effect
The range identifies the policy society should prefer
Every value in the range is equally likely.
evidence.correct_option: Uncertainty in the predicted effect
evidence.feedback: Responsible advice reports assumptions, uncertainty, and plausible unintended consequences.

evidence.stem: Two advisers share one forecast but rank equity differently. What differs?
options: Their estimates of the policy’s effects
Their normative values
Their definitions of the economic variables
One adviser must have interpreted the data incorrectly.
evidence.correct_option: Their normative values
evidence.feedback: Disagreement can reflect evidence, models, uncertainty, or different values.

evidence.stem: They agree on effects but rank fairness differently. What differs?
options: Their scientific forecasts
Their normative evaluation
One economist must have misread the data
Economic analysis cannot distinguish factual claims from value judgments.
evidence.correct_option: Their normative evaluation
evidence.feedback: Disagreement can reflect evidence, models, uncertainty, or different values.

evidence.stem: Must economist disagreement be political?
options: Yes; all disagreement among economists is ideological
No; evidence, models, or values can differ
Yes; economists using the same field must otherwise agree
Yes; empirical evidence cannot produce different interpretations.
evidence.correct_option: No; evidence, models, or values can differ
evidence.feedback: Disagreement can reflect evidence, models, uncertainty, or different values.

evidence.stem: School plan A is predicted to raise scores by 6 points and reduce free time by 4 hours weekly. Plan B raises scores by 4 points and reduces free time by 1 hour. A board declares A preferable because each extra score point is worth at least 2 hours of free time. Which assessment is exact?
options: The outcome predictions are normative; the board’s numerical weighting is positive, and A’s extra 2 points cost 3 hours.
All claims are positive because they contain numbers; A dominates B on both scores and free time.
The weighting is normative, so the score and time predictions cannot be tested against observed outcomes.
The outcome predictions are positive; the board’s weighting is normative, and A’s extra 2 points cost 3 hours relative to B.
evidence.correct_option: The outcome predictions are positive; the board’s weighting is normative, and A’s extra 2 points cost 3 hours relative to B.
evidence.feedback: Comparative predictions imply A adds 2 score points while costing 3 more hours, or 1.5 hours per extra point. Whether that is worthwhile depends on the board’s stated value criterion, not merely on the accuracy of the predictions.

evidence.stem: Suppose the only change in the gourmet-donut market is that the good's own price falls from $10 to $5. The displayed graph shows the market moving from A to B. Which conclusion is correct?
options: Quantity demanded rises 125 thousand; demand is unchanged.
Demand rises 125 thousand; D shifts right.
Quantity demanded falls 125 thousand; demand is unchanged.
Demand falls 125 thousand; D shifts left.
evidence.correct_option: Quantity demanded rises 125 thousand; demand is unchanged.
evidence.feedback: A change in the good's own price causes a movement along a fixed demand curve. Quantity demanded rises from 100 thousand to 225 thousand, but demand does not shift.

evidence.stem: Refer to the graph. Compare the initial point on D0 at $6 with the final point on D1 at $4. Which explanation correctly separates the demand shift from the subsequent price movement?
options: The shift to D1 lowers quantity at each price; moving down D1 then raises quantity to 100 thousand, only partly offsetting the shift
The shift to D1 raises quantity at each price; moving down D1 then lowers quantity to 100 thousand
Demand stays on D0 because the price fall accounts for the entire move to 100 thousand
Supply shifts left first, and movement along D1 restores quantity to 150 thousand
evidence.correct_option: The shift to D1 lowers quantity at each price; moving down D1 then raises quantity to 100 thousand, only partly offsetting the shift
evidence.feedback: At $6, shifting from D0 to D1 reduces quantity demanded. The later price decline produces movement down D1 to 100 thousand, but that movement does not fully undo the demand decrease.

evidence.stem: Refer to the graph. Calculate the quantity response per $1 price decrease from A to B, then infer which demand relationship that calculation illustrates.
options: Quantity demanded rises 25 thousand per $1 decrease, illustrating movement along a downward-sloping demand curve
Demand rises 25 thousand per $1 decrease, illustrating a rightward shift of the demand curve
Quantity demanded falls 25 thousand per $1 decrease, illustrating movement up the demand curve
Demand falls 125 thousand per $1 decrease, illustrating a leftward shift of the demand curve
evidence.correct_option: Quantity demanded rises 25 thousand per $1 decrease, illustrating movement along a downward-sloping demand curve
evidence.feedback: From A to B, price falls $5 and quantity demanded rises 125 thousand, or 25 thousand per dollar. Because the good's own price changes, this is movement along the demand curve, not a curve shift.

evidence.stem: Refer to the graph. A report attributes the entire A-to-B change to stronger tastes for donuts. A second survey finds the quantity desired at every fixed price is unchanged. Which diagnosis fits both pieces of evidence?
options: The report is supported; quantity rises 125 thousand because demand shifted right.
The report confuses movement with a shift; quantity rises 125 thousand because price is lower.
The report confuses movement with a shift; quantity falls 125 thousand because price is lower.
The report is supported; demand shifted right even though the fixed-price schedule is unchanged.
evidence.correct_option: The report confuses movement with a shift; quantity rises 125 thousand because price is lower.
evidence.feedback: A and B are on the same demand curve, at 100 and 225 thousand. The unchanged fixed-price schedule rules out a taste-driven demand shift. The graph shows an increase in quantity demanded caused by a lower price.

evidence.stem: The market begins on D0 at $6 and 150 thousand units. Demand shifts to D1 while price is still $6, and then price falls to $4. Which decomposition matches the graph?
options: 150→250 from the demand shift; 250→100 from the price fall.
150→50 from the demand shift; 50→100 from the price fall.
150→50 from the price fall; 50→100 from the demand shift.
150→100 from the demand shift; 100→50 from the price fall.
evidence.correct_option: 150→50 from the demand shift; 50→100 from the price fall.
evidence.feedback: At $6, D0 shows 150 thousand and D1 shows 50 thousand. Moving down D1 to $4 raises quantity demanded to 100 thousand. Final quantity remains 50 thousand below the starting level.

evidence.stem: The market moves from point A to point B on the displayed demand curve. What is the most precise description?
options: Demand increases, shifting D to the right.
Price falls, causing an increase in quantity demanded along D.
Price falls, causing quantity demanded to decrease along D.
Supply increases, shifting S to the right.
evidence.correct_option: Price falls, causing an increase in quantity demanded along D.
evidence.feedback: A and B lie on the same demand curve. The lower price is associated with a larger quantity demanded, so this is a movement along demand, not a shift.

evidence.stem: If coffee is a normal good, which event is consistent with the shift from D0 to D1 shown in the graph?
options: Consumer income rises
The price of coffee falls while all demand shifters stay unchanged
Coffee producers adopt cheaper technology
The price of coffee rises and buyers move up D0
evidence.correct_option: Consumer income rises
evidence.feedback: For a normal good, higher income increases demand, shifting the entire demand curve to the right.

evidence.stem: For a normal good such as tea, which change in a demand shifter could generate the illustrated curve movement?
options: The price of tea rises while all demand shifters stay unchanged
Tea producers receive a subsidy
Consumer income falls
The price of tea falls and buyers move down D0
evidence.correct_option: Consumer income falls
evidence.feedback: For a normal good, lower income decreases demand and shifts the entire demand curve left.

evidence.stem: Refer to the graph. Compare the market at $2 with the market at $4, then infer how the two opposite price-adjustment forces both move the market toward the $3 equilibrium.
options: Surplus at $2 pushes price down; shortage at $4 pushes price up.
Shortage at $2 pushes price up; surplus at $4 pushes price down.
Shortage at both prices pushes the market price steadily upward.
Surplus at both prices pushes the market price steadily downward.
evidence.correct_option: Shortage at $2 pushes price up; surplus at $4 pushes price down.
evidence.feedback: A shortage creates upward price pressure and a surplus creates downward pressure. Both adjustment forces point toward the $3 equilibrium.

evidence.stem: Refer to the graph. Compare the initial point on S0 at $9 with the final point on S1 at $13. Which explanation separates the supply shift from the subsequent price movement?
options: The shift to S1 lowers quantity at each price; moving up S1 then raises quantity back to 200 thousand
The shift to S1 raises quantity at each price; moving up S1 then lowers quantity to 200 thousand
Supply stays on S0 because the price rise accounts for the entire return to 200 thousand
Demand shifts right first, and movement down S1 restores quantity to 100 thousand
evidence.correct_option: The shift to S1 lowers quantity at each price; moving up S1 then raises quantity back to 200 thousand
evidence.feedback: The leftward shift from S0 to S1 reduces quantity supplied at each price. The later price rise causes movement up S1 until quantity supplied returns to 200 thousand.

evidence.stem: Refer to the graph. Compare point A on S0 with the final point on S1 at $2. Which explanation separates the supply increase from the later price movement?
options: The shift to S1 raises quantity at each price; moving down S1 then lowers quantity back to about 100 thousand
The shift to S1 lowers quantity at each price; moving down S1 then raises quantity to about 100 thousand
Supply remains on S0 because the price decline explains the entire move
Demand shifts left first, and movement up S1 raises quantity to about 225 thousand
evidence.correct_option: The shift to S1 raises quantity at each price; moving down S1 then lowers quantity back to about 100 thousand
evidence.feedback: The rightward shift to S1 raises quantity supplied at each price. The later price decline causes movement down S1, offsetting that increase in this particular comparison.

evidence.stem: Refer to the graph. Calculate the quantity response per $1 price increase from A to B, then infer which supply relationship that calculation illustrates.
options: Quantity supplied rises 25 thousand per $1 increase, illustrating movement along an upward-sloping supply curve
Supply rises 25 thousand per $1 increase, illustrating a rightward shift of the supply curve
Quantity supplied falls 25 thousand per $1 increase, illustrating movement down the supply curve
Supply rises 125 thousand per $1 increase because production costs decline
evidence.correct_option: Quantity supplied rises 25 thousand per $1 increase, illustrating movement along an upward-sloping supply curve
evidence.feedback: From A to B, price rises $5 and quantity supplied rises 125 thousand, or 25 thousand per dollar. Because the product's own price changes, this is movement along supply rather than a curve shift.

evidence.stem: Points A and B lie on one supply curve. What economic change occurs between them?
options: Supply increases, shifting S to the right.
Price rises, causing quantity supplied to decrease along S.
Demand increases, shifting D to the right.
Price rises, causing quantity supplied to increase along S.
evidence.correct_option: Price rises, causing quantity supplied to increase along S.
evidence.feedback: A and B lie on the same supply curve. The higher price is associated with a larger quantity supplied, so this is a movement along supply, not a shift.

evidence.stem: What does the movement from point A to point B on S0 represent?
options: An increase in supply because the supply curve shifts right.
A decrease in quantity supplied because the price is higher.
An increase in demand because buyers move along the demand curve.
An increase in quantity supplied because the price is higher.
evidence.correct_option: An increase in quantity supplied because the price is higher.
evidence.feedback: A and B lie on the same S0 curve. Price rises from $3 to $4 and quantity supplied rises from 100 thousand to 225 thousand, so this is a movement along supply.

evidence.stem: A legal maximum rent of $1,000 is shown on the apartment-market graph. How should this policy be classified?
options: Binding ceiling: $1,000 is below equilibrium.
Nonbinding ceiling: $1,000 is below equilibrium.
Binding floor: $1,000 is below equilibrium.
Nonbinding floor: $1,000 is above equilibrium.
evidence.correct_option: Binding ceiling: $1,000 is below equilibrium.
evidence.feedback: A price ceiling is binding when it is set below the market equilibrium price. The graph places the ceiling at $1,000, below the $2,000 equilibrium rent.

evidence.stem: A legal minimum wage of $10 is shown on the labor-market graph. How should this policy be classified?
options: Nonbinding floor: $10 is above equilibrium.
Binding ceiling: $10 is above equilibrium.
Binding floor: $10 is above equilibrium.
Nonbinding ceiling: $10 is below equilibrium.
evidence.correct_option: Binding floor: $10 is above equilibrium.
evidence.feedback: A price floor is binding when it is set above equilibrium. The $10 wage floor sits above the $7 market-clearing wage.

evidence.stem: Refer to the graph. Under the buyer-remitted $6 tax, buyers pay the seller $7.50 and remit $6 separately. The tax is now collected from sellers, with unchanged curves and compliance. A cinema proposes charging $13.50 plus another $6 to preserve its receipt. Which corrected invoice and burden calculation fits the same competitive equilibrium?
options: Invoice $13.50 plus $6; buyers bear $9 and sellers bear $3 relative to $10.50.
Invoice $7.50 including tax; buyers gain $3 and sellers bear $9 relative to $10.50.
Invoice $10.50 including tax; buyers bear $0 and sellers bear $6 relative to $10.50.
Invoice $13.50 including tax; buyers bear $3 and sellers bear $3 relative to $10.50.
evidence.correct_option: Invoice $13.50 including tax; buyers bear $3 and sellers bear $3 relative to $10.50.
evidence.feedback: The $6 wedge remains: buyers pay $13.50 in total and sellers retain $7.50 after remittance, at 60 thousand tickets. Seller remittance means the $13.50 invoice includes the tax. Against the untaxed $10.50 price, each side bears $3. Adding another $6 would double-count the tax and would not be the same equilibrium.
